question: Once a nitrate film has been fully copied, should an archive keep the flammable original?
answer: The original is the best evidence there will ever be. Every copy loses sharpness, tone and colour. In past decades archives copied nitrate onto safety film and then destroyed it, and modern scanners have since shown how much those copies missed. Kept cold and dry, nitrate can last well over a century.
move: Whichever side you took, it turns on what the same money would otherwise save.
counterpoint: Nitrate is a fire hazard that needs costly, specialised vaults for as long as it exists. Budgets are fixed, and every year spent guarding a film that is already safely copied is a year not spent copying one that exists only once and is decaying now. Saving the unsaved film preserves more cinema.
reference: Frick, Saving Cinema: The Politics of Preservation, Oxford University Press, 2011
